Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 350 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2019-2020) 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 350 covers ~6,223km 2 of diverse habitat which includes portions of the Central 
Mixedwood, Upper Foothills, and Lower Foothills subregions, as described by the Natural Regions Committee 
(2006). Mixedwood forests of aspen and white spruce dominate the landscape. These are interspersed with stands 
of jack and lodgepole pine as well as black spruce and tamarack muskeg.Cultivation for agricultural purposes is 
very limtted within this WMU (NW tip). Cut blocks can be found throughout the unit  along with oil and gas 
development.   
WMU 350 is delimited to the north by the shorelines of Lesser Slave Lake and the Lesser Slave River from Kinuso 
to Smith, to the west and southwest by Highway 33 from Kinuso to the Peace Pipeline west of Fort Assinibo ine, 
and to the east and southeast by the Athabasca River from Smith to the ferry on the Athabasca River west of 
Vega. For a legal definition of WMU 350 boundaries, refer to Schedule 9, part 1 of the Wildlife Regulation.  
The most recent moose survey in WMU 350 was completed in the winter of 2013-14 using Distance sampling 
methodology. The estimated moose density was 0.20 moose/km 2, and the estimated abundance was 1215 moose 
(90% CI 985 – 1500). The age-sex composition (bull:cow:calf) was 32:100:25. 
The objective of this survey was to estimate total population size (abundance), population density (moose/km 2) and 
age-sex composition ratio (bull:cow:calf) of moose to inform game management decisions.  
WMU 350 has both archery and rifle seasons for moose, the archery season is open between August 25 and 
September 23. Two limited entry riffle seasons also take place between September 24 and October 31 and 
between November 1 and November 30. 
 
Survey method 
An aerial ungulate survey was flown on February 10, 12, 13 and 14 of 2020 using Distance sampling methodology 
(Buckland et al., 2001; Thomas et al., 2010). A total of 114 parallel east-west transect lines (line length ≤ 10 km, 
interval 1.2 km, survey effort = 999.69 km) were flown over 24.9 hours with a Bell 20 6 Jet Ranger. Data were 
analyzed using the program “Distance” (Version  7.2). 
 
Results 
Snow conditions were ideal throughout the WMU and survey period, though temperatures fluctuated more than is 
ideal (-2°C to -23°C). Mild tempertures are expected to influence sightability however given the large sample size 
(249 moose groups) this potential concern was inconsequential. 
A total of 254 moose were observed in 185 groups. Of the 254 moose observed; 119 were cows, 51 were calves 
and 79 were bulls with 5 unclassifed adult moose (unknown sex). The five unclassified adults were omitted from 
the analysis.The final estimated moose density in WMU 350 was 0.48 moose/km 2 (90% CI 0.40 – 0.57), and the 
estimated abundance was 3001 moose (90% CI 2517 – 3577) with a resulting sex ratio of 66:100:43 
(bull:cow:calf).  
Given the timing of the survey most bulls had dropped their antlers. Six of the 79 bulls observed were still holding 
antlers. 
Elk occur within this unit at a low desnity, however none were observed during the survey. White -tail and mule 
deer also occur but were not classified or recorded.
